analysis.one_liner: Requires contact lens makers to sell lenses to online retailers, mail-order sellers, and pharmacies on fair terms.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate committee it was referred to and died when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the 2003 Fairness to Contact Lens Consumers Act, eye doctors must give patients their contact lens prescriptions so they can shop elsewhere. But some lens manufacturers kept their products out of cheaper channels like online stores and mail-order sellers. This bill would have required manufacturers to make every mass-market lens available on commercially reasonable, nondiscriminatory terms to any seller — eye doctors, their affiliated outlets, Internet retailers, mail-order companies, pharmacies, and warehouse stores — with the FTC writing rules and treating violations as deceptive practices. It never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 30-40 million Americans who wear contact lenses would gain access to more sellers and lower prices, since cheaper Internet and mail-order sellers could reliably get stock. Online retailers, pharmacies, and warehouse clubs would gain a guaranteed right to buy lenses.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Contact lens wearers and discount sellers

how_it_helps.text: Requires manufacturers to make every mass-produced contact lens available on commercially reasonable and nondiscriminatory terms to prescribers, entities associated with prescribers, and alternative channels of distribution — defined to include mail-order companies, Internet retailers, pharmacies, buying clubs, department stores, and mass-merchandise outlets [S3].

Directs the Federal Trade Commission to write rules to carry out the requirement within 60 days of enactment and treats violations as unfair or deceptive acts or practices, so consumers get an enforcement mechanism rather than a promise [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Contact lens manufacturers would lose control over which retailers can sell their lenses and would have to supply discount Internet and mail-order channels they had been able to keep out. FTC rulemaking and enforcement would add modest administrative costs.

drawbacks.text: The bill includes broad safe harbors: manufacturers would not have to sell to a competitor, would not have to charge everyone the same price, could refuse accounts not complying with the law, could choose whether to serve low-volume accounts directly or through distributors, and would not have to supply lenses being test-marketed in only one region — limits that blunt the nondiscrimination requirement [S3].
The bill excludes many specialty lenses, including rigid gas permeable, bifocal gas permeable, keratoconus, and custom-designed lenses, so patients with harder-to-fit eyes would not benefit [S3].

An honest supporter would acknowledge the tradeoff that forcing manufacturers to supply rival discount channels can cut into the margins that fund product research and distribution, though the bill preserves the ability to charge different prices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A modest, well-targeted consumer bill: it builds on an existing law by closing the gap where manufacturers could quietly cut off discount sellers after prescriptions were released. Its main weakness is the list of safe harbors, which lets manufacturers keep charging different prices and skip low-volume accounts, softening the guarantee for smaller online sellers. The public gain is real but narrow — cheaper lenses, not a health or income change.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee the same day, and the committee never acted on it before the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Sen. Robert Bennett, a Utah Republican, introduced the Contact Lens Consumer Protection Act on March 29, 2006, joined by Sen. Patrick Leahy, a Vermont Democrat [S3][S5].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day it was introduced [S5].
The bill had three cosponsors, two Democrats and one Republican [S4].
No further action — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — is recorded in the bill's action history before the Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Contact lens manufacturers kept their ability to decide which retailers can sell their lenses, and discount online sellers and their price-sensitive customers gained nothing.

for.name: Sen. Robert F. Bennett
for.role: U.S. Senator from Utah; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it in the Senate.

for.name: Sen. Patrick Leahy
for.what_they_did: Joined as co-introducer when the bill was introduced.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.role: Senate committee with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on March 29, 2006 and took no recorded action — no hearing, markup, or vote — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor was a Republican and the co-introducer and two of three cosponsors were Democrats, so the bill had support from both parties; its death was not a recorded party vote but inaction in committee.

industries.note: The bill would have ended manufacturers' ability to keep their lenses out of discount Internet, mail-order, and mass-merchandise channels, forcing supply on nondiscriminatory terms. Their ability to restrict distribution is the public's added cost per lens.

industries.industry: Internet retailers, mail-order sellers, pharmacies, and mass-merchandise outlets
industries.note: These alternative channels would have gained a guaranteed right to buy lenses from every manufacturer, letting them compete on price for consumers.

industries.industry: Eye care prescribers and their affiliated sellers
industries.note: The bill requires manufacturers to sell to prescribers and their associated entities, but cheaper online competition would put pressure on the lens markups that eye care practices earn from selling lenses in-office.
